chapter_theme: The invocation and first twenty verses set the book's form, three or four things each named sweet, often ranked 'foremost' (முன்) or capped with 'nothing nobler', and spread it across the king's pleasures of horse and elephant, the householder's joys of children, kin and harvest, and restraints such as not killing, not eating flesh and not looking at another's wife, which the list counts as sweetnesses rather than duties.

0.reading: The invocation names three acts of worship as sweet: reaching quickly the feet of the three-eyed god, bowing to the one who wears the ancient, glorious tulasi garland, and going with first care to praise the four-faced one.
0.nuance: The three gods are not named but are marked by their emblems: the third eye, the tulasi garland and the four faces, so the opening honours Siva, Vishnu and Brahma in turn without ranking one sect over another. The first is 'quickly' sweet (கடிதினிதே), which gives the opening its only note of urgency.

items.claim: reaching the feet of the three-eyed one is quickly sweet
worshipping the one with the ancient glorious tulasi garland is sweet
going with prior care and praising the four-faced one is sweet

1.reading: Learning even if one must go begging for it is named very sweet, offering a hand in a good assembly sweet, the speech of women whose smile is like pearls sweet, and joining those clearly superior sweet as well.
1.nuance: The first item sets learning above the shame of begging, the one thing the book elsewhere treats as a loss of dignity. நற்சலையில் in line 2 is not a known word; it reads best as நற்சவையில் 'in a good assembly', and the item is held on that reading.

items.claim: learning, even if it means entering on begging, is very sweet
lending a hand in a good assembly is very sweet, and first
the words of women with pearl-like smiles are sweet
keeping company with those who are clearly superior is sweet

2.reading: The just dealing of a man of means is named sweet; household life is foremost sweet when it is carried through in harmony; and if it does not prosper, renouncing without delay in view of impermanence is sweet above all.
2.nuance: The verse ranks the two lives by a condition: the household comes first (முன்) while it goes well, and renunciation becomes the highest sweetness (தலையாக) only when it fails, so renouncing is the remedy for a household that has not prospered, not a higher calling in itself. உடையான் வழக்கு is compressed; it may be the fair conduct of the householder (the 'one who has') or a lawsuit settled fairly, so the first item is uncertain.

items.claim: the fair dealing of the man who has property is sweet
household life is foremost sweet if it is completed in agreement
renouncing without delay, seeing impermanence, is sweet above all when the household has not prospered

3.reading: Young kin who never refuse what they are bidden are named foremost sweet, learning every day without straying into fault very sweet, the farming of a man who owns his plough sweet, and, on reflection, friendship made for a far region sweet too.
3.nuance: The four together are the supports of a house: obedient young kin, daily learning, a plough of one's own and friends abroad. The last line is compressed; தேரின் 'if one considers' and திசைக்கு 'for a region' allow the friendship to be one formed in, or for the sake of, distant parts, so the fourth item is held loosely.

items.claim: young kin who do not go against what they are bidden are foremost sweet
learning daily, without going into fault, is very sweet
farming by one who owns the plough is sweet
friendship taken for a far region, when weighed, is sweet

4.reading: Seeing an army that has elephants is named foremost sweet, not swelling one's flesh by eating flesh foremost sweet, a village on the shore of a forest river sweet, and the regard of men who have honour sweet as well.
4.nuance: The list sets abstinence from flesh between a royal spectacle and a pleasant village, as one more sweetness, and gives it the same 'foremost' (முன்) as the elephant army. It mirrors Innaa Narpathu 22 almost item for item.

items.claim: seeing an army that has elephants is foremost sweet
not eating flesh to increase one's own flesh is foremost sweet
a village on the near bank of a forest river is sweet
the esteem of those who have honour is sweet

5.reading: For a ruler the verse names as foremost sweet not killing and not granting honours by bending the sceptre, names being a just-sceptred king sweet by the means that achieve it, and calls not speaking ill of anyone good.
5.nuance: மாராயம் is the honour a king confers; the second item is about favour bestowed unjustly, not about punishment. The last item, not speaking ill of anyone, is closed with நன்கு 'good' rather than இனிது, and applies beyond the king.

items.claim: not killing is foremost sweet
not conferring honours by bending the sceptre is foremost sweet
becoming a king of the straight sceptre, by the means that achieve it, is sweet
not speaking evil of anyone is good

6.reading: Doing dharma to the extent of one's strength is named foremost sweet, the fruitful words spoken by those on the right path sweet, and taking as one's guard men who are capable and not shameless sweet.
6.nuance: வலவை usually names a shameless or wanton person; the third item asks that protectors be chosen both able (வாய்ப்புடையர்) and not of that kind, which fits a householder's or a chief's guard alike.

items.claim: doing dharma to the measure of one's capacity is foremost sweet
the fruitful words of those on the right path are sweet in their excellence

items.thing: வாய்ப்புடைய ராகி வலவைகள் அல்லாரைக் காப்படையக் கோடல்
items.claim: taking as guards those who are capable and not shameless is sweet

7.reading: The verse names brahmins' keeping of the Veda very sweet, the leading of an army by a man with bonds of loyalty foremost sweet, and not attaching oneself even to a father if he will not restrain himself sweet.
7.nuance: The first item ties Vedic recitation to a birth-group as its proper excellence. The third is the hardest claim in the chapter: it puts self-restraint above filial bond, so an unrestrained father is to be kept at a distance. பந்தம் may be the bond of loyalty to the king or the tie of kin among the troops.

norm.note: a norm of the period assigning Vedic recitation to the brahmin as his proper excellence

items.claim: brahmins' possession of the Veda is very sweet
army leadership by one with bonds of loyalty is foremost sweet

items.thing: தந்தையே ஆயினுந் தானடங்கான் ஆகுமேல் கொண்டடையா னாகல்
items.claim: not cleaving to one who will not restrain himself, even a father, is sweet

8.reading: The strength of the spirited horse one rides is named foremost sweet, seeing the fury of dark mountain-like elephants in the fierce battle of garlanded kings foremost sweet, and the eager hearing very good things without confusion sweet.
8.nuance: This is a five-line verse; the second item takes two lines. The first two items are a warrior's pleasures and the third turns to listening, so the list moves from the field of battle to the hall of learning.

items.claim: the strength of the spirited horse one rides is foremost sweet

items.thing: தார்புனை மன்னர் தமக்குற்ற வெஞ்சமத்துக் கார்வரை யானைக் கதங்காண்டல்
items.claim: seeing the wrath of dark mountain-like elephants in the fierce battle of garlanded kings is foremost sweet

items.thing: ஆர்வ முடையவர் ஆற்றவும் நல்லவை பேதுறார் கேட்டல்
items.claim: the eager hearing very good things without being confused is sweet

9.reading: The well-being of those who love us is named foremost sweet, seeing the wide moonlight in the beautiful sky sweet, and being of faultless deeds and, with tenderness, loving toward everyone sweet.
9.nuance: The list widens love outward: first the circle that loves us, then a sight open to all, then love given to everyone (யார்க்கும்), so the moonlight sits as the image between the private and the universal.

items.claim: the flourishing of those who hold us dear is foremost sweet
seeing the wide moonlight of the beautiful sky is sweet

items.thing: பங்கமில் செய்கைய ராகிப் பரிந்துயார்க்கும் அன்புடைய ராதல்
items.claim: being of flawless deeds and tenderly loving toward all is sweet

10.reading: The verse names sweet seeing that one lives without taking on debt, putting away women who lack the excellence of self-restraint, and fearing and keeping away from those of mean mind, which is sweet in every way.
10.nuance: கடம் is debt; the first item is living without borrowing. The second is a gender rule of the period: it treats a woman's நிறை as the condition of keeping her, and says nothing of the man's.

norm.note: a rule of the period that women lacking chastity or restraint are to be sent away

items.claim: seeing that one lives without incurring debt is sweet
the verse names putting away women who lack the excellence of restraint as sweet
fearing and leaving those of mean mind is sweet in every way

11.reading: Not living by going on the road is named very sweet, a keenness that does not go crooked to take sweet, and nothing is as noble as the greatness that will not eat from the hand of the unworthy even if life should go.
11.nuance: The last item is ranked by negation ('there is nothing nobler'), not called sweet, so it caps the list. அதர்சென்று வாழாமை may mean not living as a wayfaring beggar or not living by highway robbery, and உண்ணார் may be those who do not share their food or simply the base; both turn the verse on dignity, but the exact sense is uncertain.

items.claim: not living by going upon the road is very sweet
a sharpness that does not go astray to take is sweet
the greatness of not eating from the hand of the unworthy, even if life departs, is nobler than anything

12.reading: A child's living without illness is named sweet, the learning of one who does not fear the clamorous assembly sweet, and the wealth that comes to excellent men who are not fools sweet if it does not run out.
12.nuance: Each item carries a condition: the child without illness, learning without fear of the assembly, wealth without exhaustion. Sweetness is in each case the thing kept safe from its typical failure.

items.claim: a child living without sickness is sweet
the learning of one who does not fear the clamouring assembly is sweet
wealth that comes to excellent men who are not fools is sweet if it does not fail

13.reading: Not living on after honour is destroyed is named foremost sweet, living restrained so that one's gifts do not fail sweet, and possessing high wealth without a single flaw sweet for all people.
13.nuance: Verse 27 repeats the first claim in nearly the same words (மானம் படவரின் வாழாமை). தானம் may be gifts or one's standing; either way restraint is what keeps it.

items.claim: not living on once honour is destroyed is foremost sweet
living self-restrained so that one's giving does not perish is sweet
having lofty wealth without one flaw is sweet for all people

14.reading: Seeing a child's tottering walk is named sweet, hearing its babble sweeter than amrita, and having a mind that does not fear when the fruit of one's deeds arrives and burns sweet.
14.nuance: The third item turns from the nursery to adversity. வினையுடையான் is most likely the bearer of past deeds whose fruit now comes upon him; it could also be an enemy with a task in hand, so the item is held loosely.

items.claim: seeing a child's faltering steps is sweet
hearing their babble is sweeter than amrita
being undaunted in mind when one's deeds come upon one and burn is sweet

15.reading: The nobility of not looking back after another man's wife is named very sweet, rain falling on green crops suffering drought sweet, and hearing the rut-roar of mountain-like elephants at the gates of valiant kings sweet.
15.nuance: பின்னோக்கா is 'not looking after', not even turning the eye to follow her; the restraint is in the glance. Innaa Narpathu 38 names the same act from the other side.

items.claim: the dignity of not looking after another's wife is very sweet
rain pouring on green crop that suffers drought is sweet

items.thing: மறமன்னர் தங்கடையுள் மாமலைபோல் யானை மதமுழக்கங் கேட்டல்
items.claim: hearing the rut-roar of mountain-like elephants at the gates of valiant kings is sweet

16.reading: Speaking one's learning before the learned is named very sweet, joining one's betters foremost sweet, and giving of oneself without begging even a sesame's worth sweet in every measure.
16.nuance: The text reads சுற்றார்முன், which as written would be 'before those around one'; கற்றார்முன் 'before the learned' fits the sense and the Kural's phrase, and the reading here follows that, uncertainly. The third item sets giving against asking: one gives without ever asking even a little.

items.claim: setting out one's learning before the learned is very sweet
joining those greater than oneself is foremost sweet
giving without begging even a sesame-seed's worth is sweet in every measure

17.reading: Doing good to the people of the land is named sweet in every measure, winning over those who are not one's allies sweeter still, and having many kinds of grain and joining true companions drawn from many sweet.
17.domain_note: a ruler or chief: the people of his land, foes won over, granaries and allies
17.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 nearly quote Kural 679, but read நாட்டார்க்கு 'to the people of the land' where the Kural has நட்டார்க்கு 'to friends'; this may be a misprint, and on the Kural's wording the verse's audience would be anyone, not a ruler.

items.claim: doing good to the people of the land is sweet in every measure
winning over those not allied to one is sweeter still

items.thing: பற்பல தானியத்தது ஆகிப் பலருடையும் மெய்த்துணையுஞ் சேரல்
items.claim: being stocked with many grains and gathering true allies from many is sweet

18.reading: A town where the elders of the assembly live is named sweet, the excellence of ascetics who live by their discipline sweet, and rising in the morning to see one's two aged parents of unfailing worth sweet.
18.nuance: Three kinds of elder are honoured in turn: the town's elders, the ascetics, and one's own parents (இருமுது மக்கள்), and the last is placed at the start of the day.

items.claim: a town where the elders of the public hall live is sweet
the excellence of ascetics living by their discipline is sweet

items.thing: எஞ்சா விழுச்சீர் இருமுது மக்களைக் கண்டெழுதல் காலை
items.claim: rising at morning having seen one's two aged parents of unfailing worth is sweet

19.reading: Living without speaking ill of friends behind their backs is named very sweet, keeping to the truth and conducting oneself humbly foremost sweet, and, once one has made great wealth without lack, giving it where it is fit sweet.
19.nuance: வாழ்தால் in line 1 is a misprint for வாழ்தல். The gift is to go தக்குழி, 'where it is fitting', which makes the recipient's worth, not his need, the test.

items.claim: living without backbiting friends is very sweet
keeping to the truth and conducting oneself humbly is foremost sweet
giving great wealth, once made, where it is fitting is sweet

20.reading: Letting go of the fickle without approaching them is named sweet, cherishing the true words of the learned sweet, and living fittingly toward all the lives of the wide world sweet.
20.nuance: The chapter closes on the widest scope in the book so far: right conduct toward every living being of the world (மன்னுயிர்க் கெல்லாம்).

items.claim: leaving the fickle without drawing near them is sweet
cherishing the true words of the learned is sweet

items.thing: மலர்தலை ஞாலத்து மன்னுயிர்க் கெல்லாம் தகுதியால் வாழ்தல்
items.claim: living fittingly toward all the lives of the wide world is sweet

links.note: Kural 395 has the learner yearn like the poor before the rich; Iniyavai goes further and calls learning sweet even if it must be had by begging.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the poverty a simile for the learner's humility, while the verse makes it literal, so together they show the tradition moving from 'learn as if a beggar' to 'learn even as a beggar'.
links.list_adds: It puts learning got by begging first among four sweet things, ahead of the assembly and the company of the great, so the list ranks learning above the dignity it costs.

links.note: Kural 46 asks what one gains by leaving a household run in dharma; Iniyavai 2 agrees while the household goes well but makes renunciation the highest sweetness when it does not prosper.
links.teaches: Read together, the couplet's rhetorical question turns out to carry a condition: household life wins only while it succeeds, and the verse names the failure that opens the outer path.
links.list_adds: It orders household and renunciation as first and highest under a stated condition, a ranking with a hinge the couplet's question does not supply.

links.note: Kural 251 asks how one who eats flesh to swell his own flesh can have grace; Iniyavai 4 uses the same phrase and calls abstaining foremost sweet.
links.teaches: The couplet condemns the act by what it costs the eater's compassion, the verse praises the abstention as a pleasure, so the pair shows non-eating of flesh argued both as a moral loss avoided and as a gain enjoyed.
links.list_adds: It ranks abstaining from flesh 'foremost' beside the sight of an elephant army and a riverside village, so a renunciant's rule is counted among a ruler's and a villager's delights.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 22 is this verse's mirror: kings without elephants, eating flesh to swell flesh and a town cut off by a forest river are painful where elephant armies, abstaining and a town on the river's bank are sweet.
links.teaches: Side by side they show the two books built as paired catalogues, and the forest river item shows the method is not a simple negation: the same river is sweet as a bank and painful as a barrier.

links.note: Kural 323 ranks not killing first and not lying after it; Iniyavai 5 also puts not killing foremost and closes with not speaking evil of anyone.
links.teaches: Both books place non-killing at the head of a short ranked list and a restraint of speech behind it, so the pair shows the Kural's ranking reused as the frame of a king's list, where justice of the sceptre is slotted between.
links.list_adds: It sets non-killing in a king's list beside unjust honours and the straight sceptre, so a universal vow is read as the first duty of rule.

links.note: Kural 33 bids one do dharma as far as one can and without ceasing; Iniyavai 6 calls dharma done to the measure of one's strength foremost sweet.
links.teaches: The couplet sets the measure as a demand, the verse as a pleasure, so the pair shows the capacity clause working two ways: it limits what is owed and it is what makes the act sweet rather than a burden.
links.list_adds: It joins measured dharma to hearing good counsel and choosing worthy guards, so doing good is ranked first among the supports of a life rather than stated alone.

links.note: Kural 134 says a forgotten Veda can be relearned but a brahmin's birth is ruined when conduct fails; Iniyavai 7 names brahmins' keeping of the Veda as very sweet.
links.teaches: The verse praises the recitation the couplet treats as recoverable, and the couplet ranks conduct above it, so a reader sees the Kural demoting the very possession the later list holds up as the brahmin's excellence.
links.list_adds: Its own third item puts restraint above even a father, so within the list conduct also outranks the ties of birth, which brings it closer to the couplet than its first item suggests.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 28 calls painful the gallop of a spirited horse ridden by one who has not learned; Iniyavai 8 calls sweet the strength of the spirited horse one rides.
links.teaches: The same spirited horse is a pleasure or a pain according to the rider's training, so the pair locates the sweetness not in the horse but in the skill that can bear its strength.

links.note: Kural 57 says confinement is useless and a woman's own நிறை is her best guard; Iniyavai 10 calls putting away women who lack நிறை sweet.
links.teaches: The couplet moves the guard inside the woman, and the verse states the consequence when that inner guard is missing, so together they show நிறை made both the woman's defence and the ground on which she may be sent away.
links.list_adds: It sets dismissing such a wife beside living free of debt and avoiding the mean-minded, so the rule is filed among the household's protections, not among the virtues of marriage.

links.note: Kural 1065 says nothing is sweeter than thin gruel won by one's own effort; Iniyavai 11 says nothing is nobler than refusing to eat from unworthy hands even unto death.
links.teaches: Both close on the same 'nothing above it' form, but the couplet praises the food one earns and the verse the food one refuses, so the pair shows the two halves of a single code of eating with dignity.
links.list_adds: It caps a list about not living off the road and not taking crookedly with a refusal unto death, so the list climbs from avoiding gain to giving up life.

links.note: Kural 726 asks what use treatises are to those who fear the subtle assembly; Iniyavai 12 calls sweet the learning of one who does not fear the clamorous assembly.
links.teaches: The couplet denies the fearful scholar the worth of his books; the verse grants the fearless one sweetness, so the pair shows courage before the assembly as the condition on which learning pays.
links.list_adds: It sets fearless learning between a healthy child and lasting wealth, so learning appears as one of the household's goods kept safe from its typical failure.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 35 names the sickness that infants suffer as painful; Iniyavai 12 names a child living without sickness as sweet.
links.teaches: The two books say the same thing from its two sides, and the pairing shows that the child's health is the first item in the sweet list but the third in the painful one, so each book ranks it by what surrounds it.

links.note: Kural 969 likens those who die when honour is touched to the yak that dies once its hair is lost; Iniyavai 13 calls not living after honour is lost foremost sweet.
links.teaches: The couplet treats the act as a matter of nature, the verse as a pleasure chosen first, so the pair shows dying for honour justified both as instinct and as preference.
links.list_adds: It ranks death before dishonour ahead of restrained living and flawless wealth, so honour is set above the two things that would make a long life comfortable.

links.note: Kural 66 implies children's babble is sweeter than flute and lute; Iniyavai 14 calls hearing it sweeter than amrita.
links.teaches: The couplet measures the child's voice against the best of art, the verse against the food of the gods, so the pair shows the babble outranking both human and divine sweetness.
links.list_adds: It sets the babble beside the child's first steps and then beside steadiness when one's deeds come home, so the household's joys and the courage to suffer are counted together.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 38 calls painful the folly of following after another man's wife; Iniyavai 15 calls sweet the dignity of not looking after her.
links.teaches: The two lines use nearly the same words and say the same thing from two sides: what Innaa names as folly in the doer, Iniyavai names as dignity in the one who abstains, so the act is judged by its effect on the man's standing.

links.note: Kural 148 calls not looking at another's wife great manhood and full conduct; Iniyavai 15 calls not looking after her a dignity that is very sweet.
links.teaches: The couplet names the restraint a heroism, the verse a pleasure, and the verse narrows the act to the backward glance, so the pair shows the restraint tested at the smallest motion of the eye.
links.list_adds: It sets the restraint beside rain on parched crops and elephants roaring at a king's gate, so a private abstention is ranked among the large public pleasures of the land.

links.note: Kural 722 says those who make their learning go home before the learned are the learned among the learned; Iniyavai 16 calls setting out one's learning before the learned very sweet.
links.teaches: The couplet makes the act the test of reputation, the verse makes it a pleasure, so the pair shows the same performance valued as proof to others and as delight to oneself.
links.list_adds: It joins speaking before the learned to joining one's betters and giving without asking, so the list ranks learned speech first among acts of standing among superiors.

links.note: Iniyavai 17 nearly quotes Kural 679 (doing good to friends; winning over those not allied), but reads நாட்டார்க்கு, the land's people, and calls both sweet where the couplet ranks them by urgency.
links.teaches: The couplet's ranking is one of speed, the verse's one of sweetness, and the verse adds granaries and many allies, so the pair shows a counsel of timing turned into a picture of a secure ruler.
links.list_adds: It adds a third item, full granaries and true allies, so the couplet's two acts of alliance become part of a ruler's provisioning.

links.note: Kural 221 says giving to those who have nothing is the only true gift; Iniyavai 19 calls giving great wealth 'where it is fit' sweet.
links.teaches: The couplet makes need the test of a gift and the verse makes fitness of the recipient the test, so the pair shows two criteria in the tradition for where wealth should go.
links.list_adds: It places giving after making wealth without lack, and after truthfulness and humility, so giving is set as the last stage of a well-conducted life, not as an act prompted by another's need.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 32 calls painful the talk of those who speak behind one's back; Iniyavai 19 calls sweet living without backbiting one's friends.
links.teaches: They state one thing from two sides, the victim's pain and the speaker's restraint, and together show backbiting judged both by what it does to the hearer and what refraining does for the speaker.

links.note: Verse 1 names the speech of women with pearl-like smiles as sweet; verse 37 names knowing such women as poison as sweet.
links.teaches: Within one book the same object is sweet to hear and sweet to know as poison, which shows the book addressing the householder in one verse and the would-be renouncer in another rather than holding one view of women.

source_issues: Verse 1 line 2: நற்சலையில் is not a known word; read as நற்சவையில் 'in a good assembly'.
Verse 16 line 1: சுற்றார்முன் is likely a misprint for கற்றார்முன், which the sense and Kural 722 support.
Verse 17 line 1: நாட்டார்க்கு where Kural 679, which lines 1-2 nearly quote, has நட்டார்க்கு; possibly a misprint.
Verse 19 line 1: வாழ்தால் is a misprint for வாழ்தல்.
Verse 5 line 3: the line was repaired (யார்மட்டும் to யார்மாட்டும், as tamilvu); எய்துங் திறத்தால் also has an odd sandhi (expected எய்துந் திறத்தால்).
Verse 8 has five lines; the second item runs over lines 2-3.
